rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph interprets the seven fat cows and green ears as seven fertile years, and the lean cows and dry ears as seven drought years.
rows.anchor: السبع من البقرات السمان والسنبلات الخضر سبع سنين مخصبات وأما البقرات العجاف والسنبلات اليابسات فسبع سنين مجدبات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dāʾban means successive years; grammatically it is a verbal noun used nonliterally because sowing means persevering in the customary way.
rows.anchor: تدأبون كعادتكم في الزراعة سبع سنين

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Two alternative parses take dāʾban as a circumstantial accusative, meaning persistently, or as an adjective describing the seven years as continuous.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو حال أي دائبين. وقيل: صفة لسبع سنين، أي دائبة

rows.speaker: أبو حاتم
rows.claim: Abu Hatim reports Yaʿqub's hamza-vowelled reading dāʾaban and derives it from daʾiba; al-Naḥḥās says Arab linguists recognize only daʾb.
rows.anchor: وحكى أبو حاتم عن يعقوب «دأبا» بتحريك الهمزة

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ explains the vowel on the hamza as permissible because it is a guttural consonant; the root sense is habit, supported by a line using ka-daʾbika.
rows.anchor: والقول الآخر: إنه حرك لأن فيه حرفا من حروف الحلق قاله الفراء، قال: وكذلك كل حرف فتح أوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Leaving harvested grain in its ears protects it from pests and preserves it longer, as was practiced in Egypt.
rows.anchor: قيل: لئلا يتسوس، وليكون أبقى وهكذا الأمر في ديار مصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They should extract only what they need to eat; the explicit second clause is a command, while the first appears to report but may also command sowing.
rows.anchor: استخرجوا ما تحتاجون إليه بقدر الحاجة وهذا القول منه أمر، والأول خبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse grounds legal public interests: preserving religion, life, intellect, lineage, and property; securing them is benefit, losing them is harm, and averting harm is benefit.
rows.anchor: هذه الآية أصل في القول بالمصالح الشرعية التي هي حفظ الأديان والنفوس والعقول والأنساب والأموال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revealed laws guide people to worldly interests so they can know and worship God and attain afterlife happiness; this care is divine grace, not an obligation owed by God, according to Sunni authorities.
rows.anchor: ولا خلاف أن مقصود الشرائع إرشاد الناس إلى مصالحهم الدنيوية ليحصل لهم التمكن من معرفة الله تعالى وعبادته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The seven severe years are the drought years, and saying that the years eat is metaphor for their inhabitants eating the stored provisions.
rows.anchor: يعني السنين المجدبات. { يأكلن } مجاز، والمعنى يأكل أهلهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What was advanced for the years means what people stored for them; the cited poem similarly attributes sleep to night and heedlessness to day while meaning people do those things.
rows.anchor: أي ما ادخرتم لأجلهن ونحوه قول القائل

rows.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam relates from his father that Joseph noticed a man consume a double portion; when he ate it all, Joseph identified the first of the seven hard years.
rows.anchor: وحكى زيد بن أسلم عن أبيه: أن يوسف كان يضع طعام الاثنين فيقربه إلى رجل واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word qalīlan is accusative as an exception; the retained little is what people preserve as seed for sowing and thus protect their provisions.
rows.anchor: نصب على الاستثناء. { مما تحصنون } أي مما تحبسون لتزرعوا

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda glosses tuḥṣinūn as guarding or securing provisions; the wording differs but the meaning is the same.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: تحرزون. وقال قتادة: «تحصنون» تدخرون

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda glosses tuḥṣinūn as storing provisions, which supports the same sense of preserving food.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: «تحصنون» تدخرون، والمعنى واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse indicates that storing food until it is needed is permissible.
rows.anchor: وهو يدل على جواز احتكار الطعام إلى وقت الحاجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage establishes that an unbeliever's dream can be true and interpreted as seen, especially when it concerns a believer; here it is also a sign and miracle for a messenger.
rows.anchor: هذه الآية أصل في صحة رؤيا الكافر، وأنها تخرج على حسب ما رأى، لاسيما إذا تعلقت بمؤمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plentiful year was not in the king's dream; Joseph knew it through unseen knowledge granted by God.
rows.anchor: هذا خبر من يوسف عليه السلام عما لم يكن في رؤيا الملك، ولكنه من علم الغيب الذي آتاه الله

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says God gave Joseph knowledge of an extra year they had not asked about, displaying his merit and knowledge.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: زاده الله علم سنة لم يسألوه عنها إظهارا لفضله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yughāthu means people receive rain, whether derived from relief or from ghawth; the commentary distinguishes the related forms for seeking aid, relief, and rainfall.
rows.anchor: فمعنى «يغاث الناس» يمطرون

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says they will press grapes and produce oil; al-Bukhārī records this interpretation.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يعصرون الأعناب والدهن ذكره البخاري

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj reports that people will press grapes into wine, sesame into oil, and olives into oil.
rows.anchor: يعصرون العنب خمرا والسمسم دهنا، والزيتون زيتا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes the verb as milking livestock, which would indicate abundant vegetation.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أراد حلب الألبان لكثرتها ويدل ذلك على كثرة النبات

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further interpretation reads the verb as being saved or delivered, from ʿuṣra meaning refuge; Abū ʿUbayda likewise defines ʿaṣr and ʿuṣra as refuge, supported by Abū Zubayd's poetry using ʿaṣra.
rows.anchor: وقيل: «يعصرون» أي ينجون وهو من العصرة، وهي المنجاة

rows.speaker: أبو الغوث
rows.claim: Abū al-Ghawth glosses the verb as exploiting produce, from pressing grapes; iʿtaṣartu mālahu means extracting wealth from someone's hand.
rows.anchor: قال أبو الغوث: «يعصرون» يستغلون

rows.speaker: عيسى
rows.claim: ʿĪsā reads taʿṣirūn with a damma on tāʾ and fatḥa on ṣād, meaning you are rained upon, as in 78:14; another reading with kasra on ṣād has the same meaning.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عيسى «تعصرون» بضم التاء وفتح الصاد، ومعناه: تمطرون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the king's messenger arrives to summon Joseph, Joseph sends him back to ask the king about the women who cut their hands and about their situation.
rows.anchor: أي يأمره بالخروج قال: { ارجع إلى ربك فاسأله ما بال النسوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph would not leave prison until his innocence was established before the king and it was clear he had been imprisoned without a crime.
rows.anchor: فأبى أن يخرج إلا أن تصح براءته عند الملك مما قذف به، وأنه حبس بلا جرم

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: In a report from Abū Hurayra, the Prophet calls Joseph son of four noble generations and says that, had he stayed in prison as long as Joseph, he would have answered the summons; he also recites the request to investigate the women.
rows.anchor: إن الكريم ابن الكريم ابن الكريم ابن الكريم يوسف بن يعقوب بن إسحق بن إبراهيم

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Al-Tirmidhī's report from Abū Hurayra also has the Prophet praise Lot for relying on a strong support and say every prophet after him had a position of strength among his people.
rows.anchor: ورحمة الله على لوط لقد كان يأوي إلى ركن شديد

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Al-Bukhārī's report from Abū Hurayra repeats the prayer for mercy on Lot and the Prophet's statement that he would have answered the summons if imprisoned as long as Joseph; it adds that Abraham's request sought reassurance.
rows.anchor: يرحم الله لوطا لقد كان يأوي إلى ركن شديد ولو لبثت في السجن ما لبث يوسف لأجبت الداعي

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A further prophetic report calls Joseph patient and forbearing and says the Prophet would have answered the summons without seeking an excuse.
rows.anchor: يرحم الله أخي يوسف لقد كان صابرا حليما ولو لبثت في السجن ما لبثه أجبت الداعي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A similar report comes through ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Qāsim, a companion of Mālik, in al-Bukhārī's tafsir collection; it is his only report there.
rows.anchor: وروي نحو هذا الحديث من طريق عبد الرحمن بن القاسم صاحب مالك، في كتاب التفسير من صحيح البخاري

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī's version says the Prophet would have left quickly if summoned from prison and describes Joseph as forbearing and deliberate.
rows.anchor: يرحم الله يوسف لو كنت أنا المحبوس ثم أرسل إلي لخرجت سريعا

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: Another report has the Prophet marvel at Joseph's patience in interpreting the cows before securing release, and at his delaying departure when the messenger arrived.
rows.anchor: لقد عجبت من يوسف وصبره وكرمه والله يغفر له حين سئل عن البقرات

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya explains Joseph's delay as patient insistence on clearing his name before accepting royal favor, lest people forever remember the false accusation; Joseph also avoids offending the Aziz's household and honors the king's trust.
rows.anchor: كان هذا الفعل من يوسف عليه السلام أناة وصبرا، وطلبا لبراءة الساحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's choice to leave immediately and vindicate himself afterward was also sound: people may imitate these stories, and ordinary prisoners cannot know they will safely retain a chance to leave as Joseph did.
rows.anchor: فالحالة التي ذهب النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم بنفسه إليها حالة حزم، وما فعله يوسف عليه السلام صبر عظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph mentions the women collectively so that the Aziz's wife is included by implication without being named directly, a courteous and well-mannered formulation; the sentence ellipses a request to investigate them.
rows.anchor: ذكر النساء جملة ليدخل فيهن امرأة العزيز مدخل العموم بالتلويح حتى لا يقع عليها تصريح

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the king summoned both the women and the Aziz's wife, since the Aziz had died, and asked them what had happened.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: فأرسل الملك إلى النسوة وإلى امرأة العزيز وكان قد مات العزيز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khaṭb means affair or situation; the women either each tried to entice Joseph for herself or each accused the Aziz's wife of wrongdoing, which also amounted to enticement.
rows.anchor: أي ما شأنكن. { إذ راودتن يوسف عن نفسه } وذلك أن

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An alternative reading of the episode is that each woman reproached the Aziz's wife, so their words themselves constituted an enticement of Joseph.
rows.anchor: أو أراد قول كل واحدة قد ظلمت امرأة العزيز، فكان ذلك مراودة منهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥāsha li-llāh means seeking God's protection, and the women say they know no evil of Joseph, meaning adultery.
rows.anchor: أي معاذ الله. { ما علمنا عليه من سوء } أي زنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Aziz's wife sees the women admit Joseph's innocence, fears they will testify against her if she denies it, and confesses; this is God's kindness to Joseph.
rows.anchor: لما رأت إقرارهن ببراءة يوسف، وخافت أن يشهدن عليها إن أنكرت أقرت هي أيضا وكان ذلك لطفا من الله بيوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A cited line about Khudāsh uses ḥaṣḥaṣ al-ḥaqq to mean truth appearing and exposing a liar.
rows.anchor: ألا مبلغ عني خداشا فإنه كذوب إذا ما حصحص الحق ظالم

rows.speaker: أبو القيس بن الأسلت
rows.claim: Abū Qays ibn al-Aslat's verse about an egg having shaved his head witnesses ḥaṣṣ as cutting hair down to its root.
rows.anchor: قد حصت البيضة رأسي فما أطعم نوما غير تهجاع

rows.speaker: جرير
rows.claim: Jarīr's phrase al-sana al-ḥaṣāʾ describes a barren year; he substitutes wolf for hyena for rhyme, supporting the sense of a stripped or barren year.
rows.anchor: وسنة حصاء أي جرداء لا خير فيها، قال جرير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On this derivation, the truth has cut through falsehood by appearing and becoming established; the cited line uses ḥaṣḥaṣa for truth's manifestation.
rows.anchor: أي انقطع عن الباطل بظهوره وثباته

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another derivation links the phrase to ḥiṣṣa, meaning the share of truth became distinct from the share of falsehood.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو مشتق من الحصة فالمعنى بانت حصة الحق من حصة الباطل

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid and Qatāda derive the word from completely cutting hair or cutting off a portion of land; al-Jawharī also defines ḥaṣḥaṣ as gravel and stones.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد وقتادة: وأصله مأخوذ من قولهم حص شعره إذا استأصل قطعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wife's unsolicited confession displays repentance and confirms Joseph's truthfulness and honor: self-incrimination is stronger than testimony, so God combines confession with testimony to remove all doubt.
rows.anchor: وهذا القول منها وإن لم يكن سأل عنه إظهار لتوبتها وتحقيق لصدق يوسف وكرامته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nūn is geminated in khuṭbikunna and rāwadtunna because it functions like the mīm and wāw endings of masculine plural forms.
rows.anchor: وشددت النون في «خطبكن» و«راودتن» لأنها بمنزلة الميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph's question is a reminder and rebuke, fulfilling God's prediction that the brothers would later be told what they had done to him.
rows.anchor: استفهام بمعنى التذكير والتوبيخ، وهو الذي قال الله: لتنبئنهم بأمرهم هذا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan infer from their having been ignorant that the brothers were young when they seized Joseph, and not prophets; they had grown up without telling their father out of shame and fear.
rows.anchor: قال معناه ابن عباس والحسن ويكون قولهم: «وإن كنا لخاطئين» على هذا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation is that they were ignorant of the consequences of their actions.
rows.anchor: وقيل: جاهلون بما تؤول إليه العاقبة

rows.speaker: ابن إسحق
rows.claim: Ibn Isḥāq says the brothers humbled themselves by explaining their distress, Joseph felt compassion, disclosed his identity, and they asked whether he was really Joseph.
rows.anchor: فخضعوا له وتواضعوا رق لهم، وعرفهم بنفسه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One report from Ibn ʿAbbās says Joseph smiled, his teeth looked like stringed pearls, and the brothers recognized him by resemblance.
rows.anchor: ثم تبسم يوسف وكان إذا تبسم كأن ثناياه اللؤلؤ المنظوم فشبهوه بيوسف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A second report from Ibn ʿAbbās says they recognized Joseph only after he removed his crown, revealing a forehead mark like Jacob's; he raised the crown after asking what they had done.
rows.anchor: أن إخوته لم يعرفوه حتى وضع التاج عنه، وكان في قرنه علامة، وكان ليعقوب مثلها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās relates Jacob's letter recounting the trials of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and saying he had neither stolen nor fathered a thief; Joseph trembled, wept, and revealed himself.
rows.anchor: فإنا أهل بيت بلاء ومحن، ابتلى الله جدي إبراهيم بنمروذ وناره، ثم ابتلى أبي إسحق بالذبح

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr reads innaka as a declarative, though the reading may also be interrogative, as in the cited example from 26:26.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير «إنك» على الخبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: I am Joseph means I am the one wronged and intended for killing; Joseph does not say I am he, magnifying the story.
rows.anchor: أي أنا المظلوم والمراد قتله، ولم يقل أنا هو تعظيما للقصة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's favor upon Joseph and his brother means their deliverance and kingship.
rows.anchor: أي بالنجاة والملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taqwā means fearing God, while patience means enduring trials and abstaining from sins; God rewards those who patiently endure and obey.
rows.anchor: أي يتق الله ويصبر على المصائب وعن المعاصي

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr retains the yāʾ in yattaqī; this is valid if man is a relative pronoun, with yattaqī in its clause and wa-yaṣbir nominative.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير: «إنه من يتقي» بإثبات الياء

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: The retained yāʾ may also be read conditionally, with yattaqī jussive by deletion of its original final ḍamma and wa-yaṣbir either jussive or nominative.
rows.anchor: وقد يجوز أن تجزم «ويصبر» على أن تجعل «يتقي» في موضع جزم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority reading is plain; the hāʾ in innahu refers to the matter being discussed, and the clause is its predicate.
rows.anchor: وقراءة الجماعة ظاهرة، والهاء في «إنه» كناية عن الحديث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hamza in ātharaka is lightened rather than fully realized; the verb means God preferred Joseph and chose him for knowledge, forbearance, judgment, intellect, and kingship.
rows.anchor: لقد فضلك الله علينا، واختارك بالعلم والحلم والحكم والعقل والملك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Asked how the brothers could call themselves sinners despite acting deliberately, Ibn ʿAbbās answers that they knowingly acted but first missed the truth and departed its proper path.
rows.anchor: قال: وإن تعمدوا لذلك، فما تعمدوا حتى أخطؤوا الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their admission of wrongdoing carries an implicit request for pardon; every sinner has left the path of truth and fallen into doubt and disobedience.
rows.anchor: وفي ضمن هذا سؤال العفو. وقيل لابن عباس: كيف قالوا «وإن كنا لخاطئين»

rows.speaker: سفيان الثوري
rows.claim: No reproach means no blaming, rebuking, or censure today; Sufyān al-Thawrī and others give this gloss, with al-yawm meaning the present time.
rows.anchor: والتثريب التعيير والتوبيخ، أي لا تعيير ولا توبيخ ولا لوم عليكم اليوم قاله سفيان الثوري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The caravan departed from Egypt toward Syria; faṣala can be intransitive or transitive, and the father speaks to relatives who stayed behind, perhaps grandchildren, though some sons may have traveled.
rows.anchor: أي خرجت منطلقة من مصر إلى الشام، يقال: فصل فصولا، وفصلته فصلا، فهو لازم ومتعد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says a wind carried Joseph's shirt scent to Jacob across eight nights of travel.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: هاجت ريح فحملت ريح قميص يوسف إليه، وبينهما مسيرة ثمان ليال

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan estimates the distance at ten nights in one report and one month in another.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: مسيرة عشر ليال وعنه أيضا مسيرة شهر

rows.speaker: مالك بن أنس
rows.claim: Mālik ibn Anas says the shirt's scent reached Jacob by a means like the transport of Bilqīs's throne to Solomon before his glance returned.
rows.anchor: إنما أوصل ريحه من أوصل عرش بلقيس قبل أن يرتد إلى سليمان عليه السلام طرفه

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says wind fluttered the shirt and brought the fragrance of Paradise into the world to Jacob; he knew the scent could only come from that shirt.
rows.anchor: هبت ريح فصفقت القميص فراحت روائح الجنة في الدنيا واتصلت بيعقوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase innī li-ajidu means I smell, a finding through the sense of smell.
rows.anchor: أي أشم فهو وجود بحاسة الشم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid interpret tufannidūn as calling Jacob foolish, supported by al-Nābigha's use of fand for foolishness.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس ومجاهد: لولا أن تسفهون ومنه قول النابغة

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and al-Ḍaḥḥāk interpret the phrase as accusing Jacob of lying; fand means falsehood, supported by a poetic use of fand.
rows.anchor: وقال سعيد بن جبير والضحاك: لولا أن تكذبون. والفند الكذب

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr explains it as condemning Jacob or disparaging his judgment; a poet uses tafnīd for blame.
rows.anchor: وقيل: لولا أن تقبحون قاله أبو عمرو والتفنيد التقبيح

rows.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Aʿrābī, also followed by Ibn Isḥāq, takes it as weakening Jacob's opinion; fand is impaired judgment in old age.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأعرابي: «لولا أن تفندون» لولا أن تضعفوا رأيي

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda glosses the phrase as misleading Jacob.
rows.anchor: وقول رابع: تضللون، قاله أبو عبيدة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, and Mujāhid also interpret it as saying Jacob has grown old; these related explanations return to incapacitating and weakening judgment, including mistaken speech.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن وقتادة ومجاهد أيضا: تهرمون وكله متقارب المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Waraʾahu Jahannam means Hell is after the unbeliever's destruction; waraʾ can mean after, as in al-Nābigha's line that no destination lies after God.
rows.anchor: أي من وراء ذلك الكافر جهنم، أي من بعد هلاكه. ووراء بمعنى بعد

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ takes waraʾ in 2:91 as meaning something other than what preceded; Abū ʿUbayda says it means what comes after.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيد: بما بعده

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Waraʾ may instead mean in front of, supported by several poems and by the description of the king ahead of the people in 18:79; Abū ʿUbayda and Quṭrub adopt this sense.
rows.anchor: وقيل: «من ورائه» أي من أمامه، ومنه قول الشاعر

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash explains the word through idioms: something behind you will come to you, and being behind someone means pursuing him.
rows.anchor: وقال الأخفش: هو كما يقال هذا الأمر من ورائك، أي سوف يأتيك

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Naḥḥās says waraʾahu means in front of him, not as a true antonym, but because what is hidden is concealed from view.
rows.anchor: وليس من الأضداد ولكنه من توارى أي استتر

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azharī and also Abū ʿUbayda treat waraʾ as an antonym meaning either behind or in front, both rooted in concealment; Ibn al-Anbārī's explanation that Hell is hidden is judged good.
rows.anchor: وقال الأزهري: إن وراء تكون بمعنى خلف وأمام فهو من الأضداد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣadīd is water like pus by simile, or the pus and blood flowing from the people of Hell; Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb and al-Rabīʿ say it is their wash water from adulterers' genitals, while another view derives it from repelling a loathed drink.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو ما يسيل من أجسام أهل النار من القيح والدم

rows.speaker: أبو أمامة
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī cites a report from Abū Umāma, from the Prophet, concerning the verse about being given pus to drink and gulping it; the report continues in the next discussion.
rows.anchor: عن أبي أمامة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في قوله: { ويسقى من ماء صديد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yatajarraʿuhu means repeatedly sipping it in gulps because it is bitter and hot; the verb forms for gulping are related.
rows.anchor: أي يتحساه جرعا لا مرة واحدة لمرارته وحرارته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yusīghuhu means swallowing smoothly; yakādu indicates that he manages it only after delay, as in 2:71 and 22:20, which show eventual swallowing.
rows.anchor: وساغ الشراب في الحلق يسوغ سوغا إذا كان سلسا سهلا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās interprets lā yakādu yusīghuhu as being unable to get the drink down or have it pass.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: يجيزه ولا يمر به

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the causes of death reach the unbeliever from every direction, above and below and in front and behind, like the fire's canopies in 39:16.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: أي يأتيه أسباب الموت من كل جهة عن يمينه وشماله

rows.speaker: إبراهيم التيمي
rows.claim: Ibrāhīm al-Taymī says death reaches every part of his body, even the ends of his hair, because every part hurts.
rows.anchor: يأتيه من كل مكان من جسده حتى من أطراف شعره للآلام

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says death comes from every direction and place, even from the big toes.
rows.anchor: إنه ليأتيه الموت من كل ناحية ومكان حتى من إبهام رجليه

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash says the term death refers to the calamities inflicted on the unbeliever in Hell, among the greatest forms of death.
rows.anchor: يعني البلايا التي تصيب الكافر في النار سماها موتا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation says each body part faces a kind of torment that would be worse than dying repeatedly, listing bites, stings, fire, chains, boiling water, and other punishments.
rows.anchor: لا يبقى عضو من أعضائه إلا وكل به نوع من العذاب

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب
rows.claim: Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb says the unbeliever experiences repeated deaths on seeing, approaching, and drinking the requested beverage, so death reaches him without his dying.
rows.anchor: إذا دعا الكافر في جهنم بالشراب فرآه مات موتات، فإذا دنا منه مات موتات

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the unbeliever does not die and obtain relief.
rows.anchor: قال الضحاك: لا يموت فيستريح

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj says the soul remains caught in the throat, neither exiting so he dies nor returning to the body to restore life; he links this to 20:74.
rows.anchor: تعلق روحه في حنجرته فلا تخرج من فيه فيموت، ولا ترجع إلى مكانها

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other explanations say God creates pains in the body each like the pain of death, or that the death pangs are prolonged to increase torment.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يخلق الله في جسده آلاما كل واحد منها كألم الموت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The suggestion that this implies he dies is wrong: 35:36 says they are not made to die or relieved, and the unbelievers remain perpetually seized by deathlike agonies.
rows.anchor: وبذلك وردت السنة فأحوال الكفار أحوال من استولى عليه سكرات الموت دائما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the closing phrase, min warāʾihi means ahead of him, and ʿadhāb ghalīẓ is severe, continuous pain without respite, like the force meant in 9:123.
rows.anchor: أي من أمامه. { عذاب غليظ } أي شديد متواصل الآلام

rows.speaker: فضيل بن عياض
rows.claim: Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ glosses the coming grievous punishment as restraint of breath.
rows.anchor: في قول الله تعالى: { ومن ورائه عذاب غليظ } قال: حبس الأنفاس

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh parses mathalu as a subject with an omitted predicate, then restarts with their deeds are like ashes; the comparison means like a heap of ashes.
rows.anchor: قال سيبويه: ارتفع بالابتداء والخبر مضمر التقدير: وفيما يتلى عليكم أو يقص

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj supplies the sense: the example of the disbelievers in what is recited to you is their deeds, like ashes.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: أي مثل الذين كفروا فيما يتلى عليكم أعمالهم كرماد

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ allows deleting mathal so the sense is that those who disbelieve have deeds like ashes; he also offers an omitted genitive, like the deeds of those who disbelieve.
rows.anchor: وهو عند الفراء على إلغاء المثل، التقدير: والذين كفروا بربهم أعمالهم كرماد

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another parse makes mathal a predicate-like subject meaning description, or makes aʿmālahum a genitive apposition of inclusion to alladhīna.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون مبتدأ كما يقال: صفة فلان أسمر ف «مثل» بمعنى صفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage connects to 14:15: the deeds of unbelievers are null and unaccepted because they associated others with God.
rows.anchor: واتصل هذا بقوله: { وخاب كل جبار عنيد } والمعنى: أعمالهم محبطة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ashes are what remains after burning; God likens unbelievers' deeds to ashes erased by a fierce wind on a stormy day, because their deeds involved associationism.
rows.anchor: والرماد ما بقي بعد احتراق الشيء فضرب الله هذه الآية مثلا لأعمال الكفار

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: The day may be called stormy because wind occurs during it, as hot and cold days are named for their weather; alternatively day ʿāṣif can mean a day with wind, with the referenced wind omitted.
rows.anchor: أحدها أن العصوف وإن كان للريح فإن اليوم قد يوصف به لأن الريح تكون فيه

rows.speaker: الهروي
rows.claim: Al-Harawī gives the first two explanations of the day being described as stormy, including the poetic ellipsis in which a dark sun is called eclipsed.
rows.anchor: والثاني أن يريد { في يوم عاصف } الريح لأنها ذكرت في أول الكلمة

rows.speaker: الثعلبي
rows.claim: Al-Thaʿlabī and al-Māwardī give a third parse: ʿāṣif describes the wind, but follows the grammatical case of the preceding word day, like a lizard's ruined hole.
rows.anchor: والثالث أنه من نعت الريح غير أنه لما جاء بعد اليوم أتبع إعرابه

rows.speaker: ابن أبي إسحق
rows.claim: Ibn Abī Isḥāq and Ibrāhīm ibn Abī Bakr read fī yawmin ʿāṣif with the variant recorded here.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن أبي إسحق وإبراهيم بن أبي بكر «في يوم عاصف»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They means the unbelievers; in the afterlife they gain no reward from their worldly good deeds because disbelief nullified them, a loss made irrecoverable by death.
rows.anchor: يريد في الآخرة أي من ثواب ما عملوا من البر في الدنيا، لإحباطه بالكفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question about God's creation of the heavens and earth calls for inward recognition, meaning has your knowledge reached this truth? The reading khāliq is attributed to Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī.
rows.anchor: الرؤية هنا رؤية القلب لأن المعنى: ألم ينته علمك إليه؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God can remove people and bring a new creation more virtuous and obedient; replacing them with people like the first would offer no benefit, and this is not difficult for God.
rows.anchor: أيها الناس أي هو قادر على الإفناء كما قدر على إيجاد الأشياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taking people to account for their wrongdoing means punishing them immediately for disbelief and fabrication.
rows.anchor: أي بكفرهم وافترائهم، وعاجلهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase mā taraka ʿalayhā refers to the earth, though earth is unstated; the mention of creatures implies it because creatures walk on earth.
rows.anchor: أي على الأرض فهو كناية عن غير مذكور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation restricts the creatures to unbelievers; another says destroying sinful parents would mean their descendants never existed.
rows.anchor: والمعنى المراد من دابة كافرة، فهو خاص. وقيل: المعنى أنه لو أهلك الآباء بكفرهم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan takes the wording universally: God would leave no creature on earth, prophet or otherwise, if He seized all people for what they earned.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المراد بالآية العموم أي لو آخذ الله الخلق بما كسبوا ما ترك على ظهر هذه الأرض

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd says punishment for sinners would reach all creation, even beetles in their holes, stop rain and plants, and kill animals; God instead acts with pardon and grace, as in 42:30.
rows.anchor: لأصاب العذاب جميع الخلق حتى الجعلان في جحرها، ولأمسك الأمطار من السماء والنبات من الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The appointed term is the limit of a person's life; when it comes there is no delay or advance.
rows.anchor: أي أجل موتهم ومنتهى أعمارهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although collective destruction includes believers who are not unjust, the unjust die as punishment while believers receive compensation through the afterlife reward.
rows.anchor: يجعل هلاك الظالم انتقاما وجزاء، وهلاك المؤمن معوضا بثواب الآخرة

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar reports the Prophet saying that if punishment strikes a people, those present are affected and then resurrected according to their intentions.
rows.anchor: إذا أراد الله بقوم عذابا أصاب العذاب من كان فيهم ثم بعثوا على نياتهم

rows.speaker: أم سلمة
rows.claim: When Umm Salama asks about an army swallowed in the desert while pursuing a refuge seeker at the Kaʿba, the Prophet says even the reluctant are swallowed with them but resurrected according to intention.
rows.anchor: يعوذ بالبيت عائذ فيبعث إليه بعث فإذا كانوا ببيداء من الأرض خسف بهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī says he treated this issue at length in al-Tadhkira and refers readers to earlier discussions in al-Māʾida and the end of al-Anʿām.
rows.anchor: وقد أتينا على هذا المعنى مجودا في كتاب التذكرة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An alternative interpretation takes the appointed term as the Day of Resurrection.
rows.anchor: وقيل: «فإذا جاء أجلهم» أي فإذا جاء يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cattle here comprise camels, cows, sheep, and goats; they are a lesson demonstrating God's power, unity, and greatness.
rows.anchor: وهي هنا الأصناف الأربعة: الإبل والبقر والضأن والمعز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿIbra originally compares one thing with another to grasp its reality, as in 59:2; Abū Bakr al-Warrāq says the cattle's submission to people contrasts with people's rebellion against their Lord, and an innocent bearer carrying a sinner is a great lesson.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو بكر الوراق: العبرة في الأنعام تسخيرها لأربابها وطاعتها لهم، وتمردك على ربك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first reading nusqīkum, with an open nūn, is used by Medinans, Ibn ʿĀmir, and ʿĀṣim through Abū Bakr; others including Ḥafṣ use the damma form usqīkum.
rows.anchor: قراءة أهل المدينة وابن عامر وعاصم في رواية أبي بكر بفتح النون من سقى يسقي

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: The two readings may be dialectal variants; another account distinguishes giving water directly from providing a watering place or cause to drink, attributed to Ibn ʿAzīz and supported by Labīd's verse.
rows.anchor: قيل: هما لغتان. وقال لبيد: سقى قومي بني مجد وأسقى نميرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A weak variant reads tasqīkum with tāʾ, referring to the livestock, while another reads yasqīkum with yāʾ and makes God the subject; the two main forms are associated with Quraysh and Ḥimyar.
rows.anchor: وقرأت فرقة «تسقيكم» بالتاء، وهي ضعيفة

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: For the masculine pronoun in min buṭūnihi, Sībawayh says Arabs can give a singular predicate to the feminine plural cattle noun; Ibn al-ʿArabī objects that this appeal does not suit Sībawayh's rank or discernment.
rows.anchor: قيل: هو عائد إلى ما قبله وهو جمع المؤنث. قال سيبويه: العرب تخبر عن الأنعام بخبر الواحد

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says cattle, as a collective genus, may be masculine or feminine, allowing the masculine pronoun.
rows.anchor: لما كان لفظ الجمع وهو اسم الجنس يذكر ويؤنث فيقال: هو الأنعام وهي الأنعام

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī says the pronoun refers to what was mentioned; he cites the masculine pronoun in 80:11–12, and also allows the sense some of the animals since males have no milk, a view followed by Abū ʿUbayda.
rows.anchor: وقال الكسائي: معناه مما في بطون ما ذكرناه، فهو عائد على المذكور

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says cattle and naʿam are the same, and naʿam is masculine, so the pronoun returns to that masculine lexical equivalent.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: الأنعام والنعم واحد، والنعم يذكر

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabī explains masculine agreement by the collective genus sense and feminine agreement in 23:21 by the group sense.
rows.anchor: فذكره هنا باعتبار لفظ الجمع، وأنثه في سورة المؤمنين

rows.speaker: القاضي إسماعيل
rows.claim: Qāḍī Ismāʿīl infers from the masculine pronoun that a wet nurse’s husband contributes to milk kinship; the report says the woman provides milk and the man conception, and the issue is treated in 4:23.
rows.anchor: استنبط بعض العلماء الجلة وهو القاضي إسماعيل من عود هذا الضمير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Milk emerging pure between excrement and blood displays God’s power; food is processed in the stomach, milk separates from blood in veins, and excrement remains behind.
rows.anchor: نبه سبحانه على عظيم قدرته بخروج اللبن خالصا بين الفرث والدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Farth is dung that descends into the stomach; when it exits, it is no longer called farth.
rows.anchor: والفرث: الزبل الذي ينزل إلى الكرش، فإذا خرج لم يسم فرثا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās describes fodder settling in the stomach, separating into lower excrement, middle milk, and upper blood, which the liver distributes to veins and udder.
rows.anchor: فكان أسفله فرثا وأوسطه لبنا وأعلاه دما

rows.speaker: ابن بحر
rows.claim: Milk is pure from blood redness and excrement filth despite sharing one vessel; Ibn Baḥr instead glosses pure as white, supported by al-Nābigha’s verse.
rows.anchor: من حمرة الدم وقذارة الفرث وقد جمعهم وعاء واحد

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqāsh and others use the verse to argue that semen is pure, comparing it to milk emerging through the urinary tract; Ibn al-ʿArabī rejects the analogy as ignorance because milk is described as a blessing and sign.
rows.anchor: قال النقاش: في هذا دليل على أن المني ليس بنجس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī counters that semen is also a great favor because it produces honored human beings, citing 86:7 and 16:72; if impurity comes from passage through urine, it is acquired while the substance remains pure in origin.
rows.anchor: وأي منة أعظم وأرفع من خروج المني

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, Abū Thawr, and others hold semen pure; ʿĀʾisha scraped dried semen from the Prophet’s garment, and Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ also scraped it.
rows.anchor: وممن قال بطهارته الشافعي وأحمد وإسحاق وأبو ثور

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās compares semen to mucus and says to remove it with a reed or wipe it with a cloth.
rows.anchor: هو كالنخامة أمطه عنك بإذخرة وامسحه بخرقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report that ʿĀʾisha washed semen may reflect removing something distasteful rather than legally impure, reconciling it with reports of scraping.
rows.anchor: يحتمل أن تكون غسلته استقذارا كالأشياء التي تزال من الثوب لا لنجاسة

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Mālik, his school, al-Awzāʿī, and Kufans consider semen impure; reports differ from Ibn ʿUmar and ʿĀʾisha, while Mālik calls washing it from wet-dream clothing obligatory by their consensus.
rows.anchor: وقال مالك وأصحابه والأوزاعي: هو نجس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Milk from a dead animal cannot be used because a pure liquid is held in an impure udder; human milk after death is disputed according to whether a person becomes impure at death.
rows.anchor: فأما لبن الميتة فلا يجوز الانتفاع به لأنه مائع طاهر حصل في وعاء نجس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Either view on a dead woman’s milk still permits milk kinship, since a child can be nourished by it; the prophetic definition covers milk that grows flesh and strengthens bone.
rows.anchor: وعلى القولين جميعا تثبت الحرمة لأن الصبي قد يغتذي به كما يغتذي من الحية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sāʾighan means pleasant and easy to swallow; lexical forms describe drink passing smoothly, and al-Kumayt’s sawāghan is something that relieves choking.
rows.anchor: أي لذيذا هينا لا يغص به من شربه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A report says no one has ever choked on milk, and this is also attributed to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وروي أن اللبن لم يشرق به أحد قط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse permits enjoying sweetness and delicious food without opposing asceticism, provided it is lawful and not excessive.
rows.anchor: في هذه الآية دليل على استعمال الحلاوة والأطعمة اللذيذة

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: In an authentic report, Anas says he served the Prophet drinks from his cup including honey, nabīdh, milk, and water.
rows.anchor: وفي الصحيح عن أنس قال: لقد سقيت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some reciters disliked falūdhaj and milk with a meal, but most scholars permit them.
rows.anchor: وقد كره بعض القراء أكل الفالوذج واللبن من الطعام

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: When Mālik ibn Dīnār refused falūdhaj at a table, al-Ḥasan urged him to eat it, noting that cold water involved more extravagance.
rows.anchor: فأتى بفالوذج فامتنع عن أكله فقال له الحسن: كل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Abū Dāwūd and others transmit from Ibn ʿAbbās a prophetic supplication after food for blessing and better provision, and after milk for blessing and more milk because nothing else suffices for both food and drink.
rows.anchor: إذا أكل أحدكم طعاما فليقل اللهم بارك لنا فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scholars explain milk’s special status as the first nourishment, which grows bodies, sustains them, and is free of the harms of other foods.
rows.anchor: فكيف لا يكون ذلك وهو أول ما يغتذي به الإنسان وتنمي به الجثث والأبدان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary says God made milk a sign for Gabriel in guiding this community, then introduces the authentic report.
rows.anchor: وقد جعله الله تعالى علامة لجبريل على هداية هذه الأمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding discussion concludes that milk is blessed and that asking for an increase points to fertility, goodness, and abundant blessing.
rows.anchor: فهو مبارك كله

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī supplies an omitted mā after dates and grapes, with minhu signaling the ellipsis; another view supplies a generic thing, while the preferred parse takes minhu as referring to the mentioned produce without deletion.
rows.anchor: قال الطبري: التقدير ومن ثمرات النخيل والأعناب ما تتخذون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the fruit phrase may coordinate with cattle to mean there is a lesson in dates and grapes, or with the preceding min to mean drinks are also provided from fruit.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون قوله: «ومن ثمرات» عطفا على «الأنعام»

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the verse preceded wine's prohibition: sukr means wine, while good provision is lawful food and drink from the two trees; Ibn Jubayr, al-Nakhaʿī, al-Shaʿbī, and Abū Thawr agree.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: نزلت هذه الآية قبل تحريم الخمر. وأراد بالسكر الخمر

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view takes sukr as vinegar in Abyssinian and good provision as food; another takes it as sweet lawful juice that may later ferment and become forbidden when intoxicating.
rows.anchor: وقد قيل: إن السكر الخل بلغة الحبشة، والرزق الحسن الطعام

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabī calls Ibn ʿAbbās's view strongest and offers either pre-prohibition timing or a contrast between people's unlawful use and lawful use; he concludes the Meccan verse was abrogated by the Medinan wine ban.
rows.anchor: والصحيح أن ذلك كان قبل تحريم الخمر فتكون منسوخة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī says no abrogation is needed if sukr means vinegar or sweet juice, leaving the verse decisive and in force.
rows.anchor: لا نسخ، وتكون الآية محكمة وهو حسن

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Most commentators, including Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿUmar, Abū Razīn, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, Ibn Abī Laylā, and al-Kalbī, define sukr as forbidden wine and good provision as what God permits; language authorities likewise use it for wine or intoxicants, with poetry attesting sukr.
rows.anchor: إلا أن الجمهور على أن السكر الخمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Good provision means what God permits from the two fruits; another interpretation makes the clause a rhetorical question condemning the choice of intoxicants over vinegar, raisins, and dates.
rows.anchor: والرزق الحسن: ما أحله الله من ثمرتيهما

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda says sukr means taste or food, citing a poem where making someone's faults one's sukr means tasting or relishing them.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: السكر الطعم

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī chooses the food-and-drink sense: sukr and good provision name the same lawful fruit produce in different words, so there is no abrogation.
rows.anchor: وهذا اختيار الطبري أن السكر ما يطعم من الطعام

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says Abū ʿUbayda's sense is unknown and contradicts the commentators; the poem is no proof because it describes becoming intoxicated by others' faults.
rows.anchor: إلا أن الزجاج قال: قول أبي عبيدة هذا لا يعرف

rows.speaker: الحنفيون
rows.claim: The Ḥanafīs take sukr as non-intoxicating nabīdh and infer it is lawful from the verse's language of divine favor; it becomes forbidden once it intoxicates, supported by two reports about wine and diluted drinks.
rows.anchor: وقال الحنفيون: المراد بقوله: «سكرا» ما لا يسكر

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: A report attributed through ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Nāfiʿ says Ibn ʿUmar saw the Prophet dilute a strong drink with water until it was drinkable and advise breaking the vessels' strength with water.
rows.anchor: رأيت رجلا جاء إلى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وهو عند الركن

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet drank the prepared nabīdh that day and gave it to a servant after it changed on the second or third day; the author uses this to argue it was not forbidden.
rows.anchor: وروي: أنه عليه السلام كان ينبذ له فيشربه ذلك اليوم، فإذا كان من اليوم الثاني أو الثالث سقاه الخادم إذا تغير

rows.speaker: الطحاوي
rows.claim: Al-Ṭaḥāwī cites a report from Ibn ʿAbbās that wine itself, little or much, is forbidden, whereas intoxicating drinks other than wine are not forbidden by their essence.
rows.anchor: حرمت الخمر بعينها القليل منها والكثير والسكر من كل شراب

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: A report from ʿUmar says nabīdh is what cuts camel meat in the stomach; al-Sawrī was also seen drinking nabīdh at Mālik ibn Maʿwal's home.
rows.anchor: إنا نأكل لحوم هذه الإبل وليس يقطعه في بطوننا إلا النبيذ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Ḥanafī argument from divine favor is sound in itself but may refer to the period before wine was prohibited, making the verse abrogated as explained earlier.
rows.anchor: فيكون منسوخا كما قدمناه

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabī argues that reports containing legal judgments can be abrogated because the report entails a legal demand; only reports of actual facts or divine reward are not abrogated.
rows.anchor: فأما إذا تضمن الخبر حكما شرعيا فالأحكام تتبدل وتنسخ، جاءت بخبر أو أمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī calls Ibn al-ʿArabī's polemic against opponents excessive, but agrees that the correct legal-theory position allows abrogating a report about a ruling, supported by 16:101.
rows.anchor: قلت: هذا تشنيع شنيع حتى يلحق فيه العلماء الأخيار في قصور الفهم بالكفار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first two reports used by the Ḥanafīs are weak; stronger prophetic reports state that every intoxicant is forbidden and that what intoxicates in large quantity is forbidden in small quantity, with al-Nasāʾī defending the transmitters' reliability.
rows.anchor: وأما ما ذكروا من الأحاديث فالأول والثاني ضعيفان لأنه عليه السلام قد روي عنه بالنقل الثابت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third report is authentic but the Prophet gave the changed-smelling nabīdh to a servant because he disliked its odor, not because it intoxicated; the same concern explains the report about Zaynab's honey and maghāfīr.
rows.anchor: وأما الثالث وإن كان صحيحا فإنه ما كان يسقيه للخادم على أنه مسكر

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās is also reported by ʿAṭāʾ, Ṭāwūs, and Mujāhid to say that what intoxicates in quantity is forbidden in small quantity; this is also related by Qays ibn Dīnār and is his legal opinion.
rows.anchor: ما أسكر كثيره فقليله حرام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report through ʿAbd Allāh ibn Shaddād conflicts with the larger group and established prophetic teaching, so it cannot support the opposing position.
rows.anchor: وقد خالفه الجماعة، فسقط القول به مع ما ثبت عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: ʿUmar's nabīdh meant a non-intoxicating drink; al-Nasāʾī reports it had been turned into vinegar, and another report says ʿUmar punished a drinker if the drink proved intoxicating.
rows.anchor: كان النبيذ الذي شربه عمر بن الخطاب قد خلل

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: In a sermon, ʿUmar says wine's prohibition covers drinks made from grapes, honey, dates, wheat, and barley, and defines wine by its effect on the intellect.
rows.anchor: أما بعد، أيها الناس فإنه نزل تحريم الخمر

rows.speaker: إبراهيم النخعي
rows.claim: Al-Nasāʾī says Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī was the first to permit intoxicating nabīdh; al-Qurṭubī calls this a learned scholar's error and says no opinion overrides the Sunna.
rows.anchor: ذكر النسائي في كتابه أن أول من أحل المسكر من الأنبذة إبراهيم النخعي

rows.speaker: ابن المبارك
rows.claim: Ibn al-Mubārak says the only reliably transmitted concession for intoxicants was from Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī.
rows.anchor: ما وجدت الرخصة في المسكر عن أحد صحيحا إلا عن إبراهيم

rows.speaker: الطحاوي
rows.claim: Even if reports of al-Ṭaḥāwī or al-Thawrī permitting it are sound, they cannot override the Sunna; al-Ṭaḥāwī elsewhere says the community agrees that fermented, foaming grape juice is wine and that permitting it is unbelief, while date-wine is disputed.
rows.anchor: اتفقت الأمة على أن عصير العنب إذا اشتد وغلى

rows.speaker: الطحاوي
rows.claim: Al-Ṭaḥāwī argues that the report calling wine a product of date palm and grape was not acted upon as applying the prohibition to date wine; nevertheless, the jurists analogize intoxicating date and raisin infusions and thus every intoxicating drink.
rows.anchor: الخمر من هاتين الشجرتين النخلة والعنب

rows.speaker: الطحاوي
rows.claim: Al-Ṭaḥāwī accepts the report that every intoxicant is forbidden but says scholars differ whether it means the whole category that can intoxicate or only a drink that actually causes drunkenness.
rows.anchor: كل مسكر حرام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī concludes that al-Ṭaḥāwī's own reasoning makes every intoxicating drink prohibited.
rows.anchor: قلت: فهذا يدل على أنه محرم عند الطحاوي لقوله، فوجب قياسا على ذلك أن يحرم كل ما أسكر

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: ʿĀʾisha says wine is forbidden for its consequence rather than its name, so every drink with the same consequence is forbidden.
rows.anchor: إن الله لم يحرم الخمر لاسمها وإنما حرمها لعاقبتها

rows.speaker: ابن المنذر
rows.claim: Ibn al-Mundhir says the Kufans brought defective reports; disputes must return to Qur'an and Sunna, and a successor's drinking is either mistaken interpretation or a sin requiring repentance.
rows.anchor: وجاء أهل الكوفة بأخبار معلولة، وإذا اختلف الناس في الشيء وجب رد ذلك إلى كتاب الله وسنة رسوله

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An alternative interpretation treats the fruits as evidence for resurrection: their Creator can resurrect, regardless of whether wine is lawful, and mentioning its use does not itself imply prohibition, as in 2:219.
rows.anchor: إنها إنما ذكرت للاعتبار، أي من قدر على خلق هذه الأشياء قادر على البعث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ardhal al-ʿumur means the worst and lowest age, when strength and intellect decline into senility and the like.
rows.anchor: يعني أردأه وأوضعه. وقيل: الذي ينقص قوته وعقله ويصيره إلى الخرف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās calls it the lowest stage of life, when a person becomes like a child without reason.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: يعني إلى أسفل العمر، يصير كالصبي الذي لا عقل له

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Al-Bukhārī reports from Anas that the Prophet sought refuge from laziness, cowardice, senility, and miserliness; a report from Saʿd adds seeking refuge from being returned to the lowest age.
rows.anchor: اللهم إني أعوذ بك من الكسل وأعوذ بك من الجبن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Not knowing after knowledge means returning through extreme old age to childhood and forgetting matters once known.
rows.anchor: أي يرجع إلى حالة الطفولية فلا يعلم ما كان يعلم قبل من الأمور

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view says this loss of knowledge does not happen to a believer because a believer's knowledge is not taken away.
rows.anchor: وقد قيل: هذا لا يكون للمؤمن، لأن المؤمن لا ينزع عنه علمه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another reading of the meaning is that the person no longer acts after knowing; action is expressed as knowledge because it depends on knowledge, and age affects action more.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المعنى لكيلا يعمل بعد علم شيئا فعبر عن العمل بالعلم لافتقاره إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The argument addresses deniers of resurrection: the One who returns a person to this condition can cause death and then bring him back to life.
rows.anchor: والمعنى المقصود الاحتجاج على منكري البعث، أي الذي رده إلى هذه الحال قادر على أن يميته ثم يحييه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hand shackled to the neck is a metaphor for the miser whose will cannot release anything from his wealth, like a shackle restraining the hand.
rows.anchor: هذا مجاز عبر به عن البخيل الذي لا يقدر من قلبه على إخراج شيء من ماله

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: In Bukhārī and Muslim, Abū Hurayra reports the Prophet's parable of miser and giver in iron cloaks: charity loosens the giver's clothing while the miser's rings tighten; Abū Hurayra saw the Prophet gesture to show it.
rows.anchor: ضرب رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم مثل البخيل والمتصدق كمثل رجلين عليهما جبتان من حديد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Stretching the hand fully pictures losing one's wealth: a closed fist retains what it holds, while an open hand lets it go.
rows.anchor: ضرب بسط اليد مثلا لذهاب المال، فإن قبض الكف يحبس ما فيها، وبسطها يذهب ما فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although addressed to the Prophet, the verse means his community, since scripture often uses their leader as their representative in Arab usage.
rows.anchor: وهذا كله خطاب للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم والمراد أمته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet saved nothing for the next day and endured hunger, while some Companions spent all their wealth; he did not condemn them because of their certainty and insight.
rows.anchor: فإنه عليه الصلاة والسلام لم يكن يدخر شيئا لغد، وكان يجوع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition targets excessive spending by someone who fears regret over what he gave away; one who trusts God's promise and reward is outside the intended warning.
rows.anchor: وإنما نهى الله سبحانه وتعالى عن الإفراط في الإنفاق، وإخراج ما حوته يده من المال

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view makes the address specific to the Prophet, teaching him moderation in spending.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن هذا الخطاب للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في خاصة نفسه، علمه فيه كيفية الإنفاق

rows.speaker: جابر
rows.claim: Jābir and Ibn Masʿūd relate that a boy requested a shirt for his mother, so the Prophet gave his own and remained at home without clothes until people entered and found him naked; the passage says the verse was revealed then.
rows.anchor: فخلع قميصه فدفعه إليه وجلس في البيت عريانا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These instructions concern charitable spending; spending on corruption is forbidden whether little or much.
rows.anchor: وكل هذا في إنفاق الخير. وأما إنفاق الفساد فقليله وكثيره حرام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse discourages exhausting one's resources in response to the first needy person, lest later people or one's dependents be left without support; a maxim says every extravagance has a neglected right, and the ruling depends on each person's circumstances.
rows.anchor: نهت هذه الآية عن استفراغ الوجد فيما يطرأ أولا من سؤال المؤمنين لئلا يبقى من يأتي بعد ذلك لا شيء له

rows.speaker: ابن عرفة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿArafa says one who squanders wealth ends up exhausted and unable to spend or act, like a spent camel; 67:4 uses ḥasīr for a tired, depleted gaze.
rows.anchor: يقول لا تسرف ولا تتلف مالك فتبقى محسورا منقطعا عن النفقة والتصرف

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda interprets maḥsūran as regretting what one has spent; al-Qurṭubī objects that the active form for regret is ḥasir or ḥasrān, not maḥsūr.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: أي نادما على ما سلف منك فجعله من الحسرة وفيه بعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person is malūm if blamed for wasting wealth or if denied assistance by someone who reproaches him.
rows.anchor: والملوم: الذي يلام على إتلاف ماله، أو يلومه من لا يعطيه
